title: The man who fooled the art world

paragraphs: In 1945, shortly after the end of the Second World War, Dutch police arrested a painter called Han van Meegeren. The charge was extremely serious: he had sold a national treasure, a painting by the seventeenth-century master Johannes Vermeer, to the Nazi leader Hermann Göring. If he was found guilty of collaborating with the enemy, he could face the death penalty.

After several weeks in prison, van Meegeren made a startling confession. The painting was not a Vermeer at all. He had painted it himself, along with several other "Vermeers" that hung in famous collections, including one that a Rotterdam museum had proudly bought in 1937.

At first, nobody believed him. So, to prove his claim, he painted another fake Vermeer in front of witnesses. The story turned him from a traitor into something close to a folk hero: the man who had tricked Göring.

How had he fooled so many experts? Van Meegeren was a skilled painter who felt that critics had never recognised his talent. He studied Vermeer's technique in depth, bought old canvases from the period and used pigments that would have been available in the seventeenth century. He also developed a method of hardening the paint by baking it, so that it would look centuries old. Crucially, rather than copying known works, he painted religious scenes that experts had long believed Vermeer must have produced early in his career. His fakes, in a sense, told the experts exactly what they wanted to hear.
In 1947, he was convicted not of collaboration but of forgery and fraud, and sentenced to one year in prison. He never served it: he died of a heart attack a few weeks later.

Today, his forgeries look surprisingly unlike Vermeer to many viewers; the faces, for instance, seem to belong more to the 1930s than to the 1600s. The case is often used to show how expectations, reputation and wishful thinking can influence even the most expert eyes.
